title: Formula Errors, IFERROR & Auditing
goal: Read what each # error is telling you, fix the common ones, use IFERROR for clean output without hiding real bugs, and audit a sheet by showing its formulas.

steps.text:
An error isn't Excel breaking. It's Excel telling you **why** it couldn't work something out, and the word after the `#` is the clue:

• `#DIV/0!`: dividing by zero (or by an empty cell)
• `#N/A`: a lookup couldn't find what you asked for
• `#VALUE!`: a calculation hit text where it needed a number
• `#REF!`: the formula points at a cell that was deleted
• `#NAME?`: Excel doesn't know a name, usually a typo

See ==D2==: Pens has a Qty of 0. Click the button to give it a real quantity.

steps.prompt:
This Total shows `#NAME?`. Excel doesn't know a function called `SUMM`.

Fix the formula in ==B5== so it adds the three costs.
steps.explain: **650.** `#NAME?` nearly always means a typo in a function name (or text without quotes). Tip: as you type a function name, Excel lists matches. Press [[Tab]] to accept one and you'll never mistype it.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use the real function name, **SUM**, to add the costs.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The costs are in `B2:B4`. Make sure the function name is spelled exactly `SUM`.

clues: The name has one M, not two.

steps.prompt:
`D2` shows `#VALUE!` because Pens' quantity is **“12 pcs”**, which is text. Multiplying text fails.

Fix the data: click ==B2==, type just **12**, press [[Enter]].
steps.explain: Once `B2` is a true number, `D2` works out **12 × 5 = 60**. Units like “pcs” belong in the header, not in the cell. A hidden space or a number typed as text causes `#VALUE!` the same way.

wrongFeedback.textNotNumber: Still text. Type only the digits **12**: no “pcs”, no spaces.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: `B2` should be **12**. Click it and type again.

steps.prompt:
The Total used to be `=B2+C2`. After a tidy-up it shows `#REF!`.

What happened?
options: Someone deleted the column the formula pointed to
steps.explain: The formula pointed at `C2`, then column C was **deleted**, and `#REF!` replaced the address. Fix: press [[Ctrl]] + [[Z]] straight away to undo the delete, or retype the formula with the right cells.
wrongFeedback: Excel handles huge numbers fine. A `#REF!` is about a **reference** to a cell.
Dividing by zero gives `#DIV/0!`. `#REF!` means a cell that was pointed to has gone.
clues: `REF` is short for reference: the address in the formula.

steps.prompt:
A lookup formula is hunting for **Mango** in the fruit list, and shows `#N/A`.

What is it telling you?
options: The thing being looked up isn't in the list
The price is text, not a number
steps.explain: `#N/A` means “not available”: Mango isn't in `A2:A4`. Before blaming the formula, check the spelling and look for extra spaces in the word being searched for.
wrongFeedback: A deleted cell gives `#REF!`. `#N/A` is a lookup saying “I couldn't find it”.
Text where a number is needed gives `#VALUE!`. `#N/A` is about not finding the item.

steps.prompt:
Chai had **0** visitors, so dividing by zero gives `#DIV/0!` in the Per visitor column. A report full of errors looks bad.

**IFERROR** takes a formula, plus what to show if it fails: `=IFERROR(formula, backup)`. In ==D3==, type `=IFERROR(B3/C3,"No visitors")`.
steps.explain: `400 ÷ 0` would be `#DIV/0!`, so IFERROR shows its backup, **No visitors**. For Tea, the same formula would simply give 12, because no error happens.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and put quote marks around the words.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Chai has 0 visitors, so the backup message should appear. The formula is `=IFERROR(B3/C3,"No visitors")`.

clues: `=IFERROR(` the division, a comma, the backup in quotes, `)`.

steps.prompt:
The backup can be a number too, and then it needs **no quotes**.

A shop's **Rate** is Orders ÷ Visits. Nobody visited on Tuesday, so the rate is an error. In ==D3==, show **0** instead.
steps.explain: Tuesday has 0 visits, so `0 ÷ 0` would be `#DIV/0!`. IFERROR swaps it for a plain **0** that later totals and averages can still use.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and commas. A number backup needs no quotes.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Divide Orders by Visits (`C3/B3`), and give `0` as the backup.

steps.prompt:
Meera's three taxi fares total **270**. She types `=IFERROR(SUMM(B2:B4),0)`, with the typo from earlier, because “IFERROR makes errors go away”.

What will her Total cell show?
steps.explain: `SUMM` fails with `#NAME?`, and IFERROR **swallows** any error, so the cell quietly shows **0**. Nothing looks broken, but the total is wrong. Let's catch it.
wrongFeedback: That's what you'd see **without** IFERROR. IFERROR catches every kind of error, typos included.
IFERROR can't repair the typo. It only replaces the error with the backup, **0**.
clues: What does IFERROR do when the formula inside it fails?

steps.prompt:
Here's Meera's sheet. The total says **0**, but the fares add up to 270.

Fix ==B5== with a plain formula, so the typo can't hide.
steps.explain: **270.** Only use IFERROR where you **expect** an error, like dividing by a possible zero. Wrapped around everything, it hides real mistakes. First make the formula work, then decide if it needs a safety net.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The total should be 270. Spell the function `SUM`, then the fares in `B2:B4`.

clues: Drop the IFERROR wrapper and correct the name.

steps.prompt:
To audit a sheet you'd like to see every formula **at once**, not click cell by cell.

Press [[Ctrl]] + [[`]]: the key above [[Tab]], left of [[1]]. Press it again to switch back. On a Mac it's [[Control]] + [[`]].

In Excel, this flips every cell between its **answer** and its **formula**.
clues: It's the backtick key, usually top-left of the keyboard under Esc.

steps.prompt:
Your Total looks wrong and you want arrows drawn from it to **the cells that feed it**.

Which command does that? (**Formulas** tab → **Formula Auditing** group)
steps.explain: **Trace Precedents** draws arrows **from the cells a formula uses** to the formula. Select `D4`, then use [[Alt]], [[M]], [[P]] to see arrows from `D2` and `D3`. **Trace Dependents** goes the other way: which formulas use the selected cell.
wrongFeedback: Close, but that's the reverse: Dependents show which formulas **use** the selected cell. You want the cells that feed `D4`.
Show Formulas replaces every answer with its formula text, but it doesn't draw arrows to the cells.
clues: “Precedents” come **before**: they're the cells that feed the formula.

steps.prompt:
Each class's average is its Total marks divided by its number of Students. **Class C** has no students yet, so its average would be an error.

In `D4`, work out Class C's average, but show the words **No students** instead of an error.
steps.explain: **No students.** Class C divides by 0, a `#DIV/0!` that you **expected**, so a safety net is the right tool. The same formula copied down would still work out proper averages for A, B and D.

wrongFeedback.missingReference: Divide Class C's Total marks by its Students, using `B4` and `C4`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and put quote marks around the words.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The cell must show the words **No students**, not an error. Wrap the division with a backup.

clues: Marks ÷ Students is `B4/C4`; give that a backup in case it fails.
